articles.body: Looking for a ChatGPT-style experience without being locked into one provider? The open-source ecosystem has plenty of options — maybe too many. 😅 I mapped 51 apps and compared 12 across 64 selection criteria, including: 🧠 Coding, research, and document chat 🔒 Privacy, telemetry, and offline use 🖥️ Desktop, mobile, and self-hosted deployment 🛠️ MCP support and AI agents 👥 Team features and administration 📜 Licensing and project activity The results highlight some useful distinctions. Open WebUI is a strong all-rounder for self-hosted use, DeepChat stands out among installable desktop apps, and Jan and PocketPal AI are worth a look for private, offline workflows. But stars aren't quality scores, and feature counts aren't universal verdicts.

articles.title: Recursive Governance: When Agents Write the Rules They Execute
articles.excerpt: We almost lost forty modules to a file that never changed. The sync job ran every six hours, mirroring our shared working directory into a test workspace. At 21:47 on a Tuesday, it removed about forty…
articles.body: We almost lost forty modules to a file that never changed. The sync job ran every six hours, mirroring our shared working directory into a test workspace. At 21:47 on a Tuesday, it removed about forty private modules that should have been ignored. The filter file was missing one pattern. That's it. One pattern. A colleague had restructured the source tree three days earlier, added a directory, and didn't update the filter file. The script didn't warn, didn't ask, didn't fail. It just mirrored the state it was told to mirror. Restoring the modules took us almost two hours, one by one from the backup box. The filter file was a static text file. It encoded what the sync could delete and what it couldn't, and it had no idea that the real inventory had changed.

articles.title: Batch-processing product photos to a clean white background: a 3-pass workflow
articles.excerpt: If you shoot a whole catalog in one afternoon, editing one photo at a time is where the evening goes. Here is the batch workflow we use to take a folder of product shots to storefront-ready white back…
articles.body: If you shoot a whole catalog in one afternoon, editing one photo at a time is where the evening goes. Here is the batch workflow we use to take a folder of product shots to storefront-ready white backgrounds — three passes, most of it automated. Pass 1 — triage the folder (2 minutes) Open the folder and sort by shooting setup, not by product. All photos from the same light and angle belong in one batch: a tool that keys a white background calibrates per batch, and mixed setups in one batch produce inconsistent edges. Delete obvious rejects now (motion blur, lens cap still on) instead of paying processing time on them.

articles.title: 'They're kind of goth': NASA spacecraft gives mysterious brown dwarfs a close-up
articles.excerpt: Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a horde of mysterious "failed stars," or brown dwarfs, not-so-stellar loners that wander the darkness of space alone.
articles.body: Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a host of "failed stars," also known as brown dwarfs. These strange cosmic bodies straddle the line between planets and stars, possessing a mass between 13 and 80 times that of Jupiter (0.013 to 0.08 times the mass of the sun ). They get the nickname failed stars because they form like stars from collapsing clouds of gas and dust but fail to gather enough mass to trigger the fusion of hydrogen to helium in their cores, the process that powers actual stars . This formation process also means that brown dwarfs are cosmic loners, wandering the darkness of space alone, bereft of the light of a parent star. That description might sound like lyrics from a Type O Negative song ("Black No. 1," anybody?).

articles.body: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France.

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.

articles.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
articles.excerpt: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
articles.body: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own.
